Map its reasons in a Whybase proposition tree -- a recursive proposition tree where each atomic statement is proposition with one or more premises (atomic statements, which also stand alone as propositions). Then I map each statement to the relevant code, hinted at by tool calls and git commits. Every time an agent touches that file or directory, a hook triggers in Claude Code that queries the codegraph db for the mapped statements. topComments.text: Gaming magazines were THE best part of my life growing up. More than the games themselves, more than cartoons, more than family, friends (I had none..the reviewers were my friends :) We lived in the backwater town of a backwater country, going through a turbulent era. There was nothing to buy there, except local food and produce and clothes. The only foreign stuff available to buy were the absolute basics like soaps and shampoo, and pirated movies and music on cassette tapes (even there people knew and adored Michael Jackson!) The nearest city with international imports was 10-12 hours away on bus. Sometimes my uncle would go there for work, and the thing I looked forward to the most were the MAGAZINES he would bring back. I would pore over them again and again, and fantasize about the games in them… it would be months before my uncle went again. So I made wishlists, drew comics about the stuff in those magazines, and learned English and about the rest of the world from them. At first it was Sinclair User, Your Sinclair, then ZZAP!64. I picked up British humor from them, that still colors mine to this day. :) I learned about the USSR through Raid Over Moscow, the Vietnam War through Rambo and Platoon, the Falklands through some wargames, and other things that I would not be able to make sense of until decades later. Every magazine and every reviewer, even the imaginary ones like Chuck Vomit the troll who reviewed text adventure games, had an intensely unique personality that affected how people perceived the games they were reviewing. The 1980s and early 1990s magazine subculture is the most sorely missed aspect of gaming and computing that was lost when the internet took over. Even if you didn't grow up on them, do flip through some random pages of the aforementioned magazines, just to see how some things never changed: There were PC vs Mac wars and console wars even back in 1985! There were people worrying about how increasingly powerful computers would make everyone dumber even back then!

topComments.author: boricj
topComments.text: That reminds me of some of the tricks I've used while tinkering with a voxel space rendering tech demo on the PlayStation. The quirks of that console for this is that the CPU takes a 6 cycle stall on any read from main RAM (it's not even stall-on-use) and doesn't have a data cache. That would make it a very poor fit for this, so I had to improvise a bunch of tricks to reclaim performance: - Made all of my hot loop fit within one function, so that it fits entirely in the 4 KiB direct-mapped instruction cache (so less than 1024 instructions) - Wrote a C++ template that can trampoline a function call into the 2 KiB scratchpad - Used the rest of the scratchpad for a CLUT table because it doesn't stall on read - Used the GTE to transform the N set of coordinates while the CPU stalls fetching the N+1 set of heightmap data - Figured ways to abuse the GTE into transforming more points per instructions than it theoretically can, taking advantage of simplified formulas compared to real 3D projection - Write the rectangle primitives straight to the GPU registers instead of going through a display list It's such an abuse of the PlayStation that PCSX-Redux and DuckStation disagree on its performance by up to a factor of two. I should finish it someday and see how it runs on real hardware...

jobs.text: I’m Chris, VP Engineering at Fazeshift. stackOverflowQuestions.title: What should I do when a REST request times out but the operation may still be running?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I have a Spring Boot service that calls another API to start an operation that can take a few minutes. Something like: My service -> POST /operations -> Provider Normally, the provider returns an operationId , which I store and then use to check the status of the operation later. The part I'm struggling with is what to do when the initial POST request times out. For example, the provider might actually receive the request and successfully start the operation, but the response gets lost somewhere. Now my service has no way of knowing whether the operation was created or not. If I retry the POST, I could end up creating a duplicate operation. But if I don't retry, I might leave a perfectly valid operation running in the provider without ever knowing its operationId . How should I design this?

stackOverflowQuestions.title: Declaring a С++ operator function that is friend to a class
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: How can I make the Counter class's operator+ function access the private int value variable? After all, that requires making the function a friend —meaning it must be declared before the class definition and then specified inside the class—but the compiler won't know the function's type at that point. #include <iostream> Counter operator + (const Counter& c1, const Counter& c2); class Counter { friend Counter operator + (const Counter& c1, const Counter& c2); public: Counter(int val){ value = val; } void print(){ std::cout << value << std::endl; } private: int value; }; Counter operator + (const Counter& c1, const Counter& c2) { return Counter{c1.value + c2.value}; } int main(){ Counter c1 {10}; Counter c2 {15}; Counter c3 = c1 + c2; c3.print(); }
